subject: English Literature
board: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE (9-1) in English Literature (4ET1)
source: Gap-fill against Pearson Edexcel International GCSE English Literature 4ET1 specification

lessons.unit: Unit 1A: Component 1 Section A: Unseen poetry
lessons.title: Unseen poetry: the Pearson question, what it rewards and how to prepare
lessons.bigQuestion: What does a poem you have never seen ask you to do, and what does it not ask?
objectives: State the format of Section A: one 20-mark essay on one unseen poem, assessed for AO2
Explain what AO2 rewards and what the question does not reward
Plan a reading habit using a selection of modern poetry
successCriteria: All: say what Section A asks and how many marks it carries
Most: use a focus list (imagery, language, tone, mood, structure, form) to annotate a poem
Some: write a first paragraph that links a technique to its effect
lessons.crossCurricular: Wider reading: modern poets across cultures; PSHE: managing exam nerves
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: attentiveness and careful reading, echoing the Quranic call to reflect

keywords.def: a poem printed on the paper that you have not studied in class
analysing the writer's language, form and structure and the effects they create
language that creates pictures or sensory impressions
the attitude the speaker seems to have
the feeling the poem creates in the reader
the shape and type of a poem, such as sonnet or free verse

starter: Bismillah. Name two features of a sonnet.
What is the difference between tone and mood?
Give one example of imagery from any poem you know, without quoting more than three words.

teach.heading: What Section A asks
teach.note: Spell out the facts from the specification: Component 1 Section A is a single 20-mark essay on one unseen poem, and the poem is printed in the question paper. It is assessed only for AO2. Ask: if there is no AO3 or AO4 here, what can you leave out? Answer: comparison and context. Reassure pupils that no prior knowledge of the poem is needed. Timing is a recommendation: marks are 20 out of 90 for a 2-hour paper, so roughly 25-30 minutes if you share time by marks (approx.).
bullets: One unseen poem, printed on the paper
No comparison and no context needed

teach.heading: Focus list for AO2
teach.note: Teach the focus list straight from the specification: imagery, language choice, tone, mood, structure, form and literary terminology. Each is a lens, not a checklist to tick. Pupils choose the lenses that fit THIS poem. Ask which two lenses they would use on a poem with no rhyme and very short lines.

head: Lens
Question to ask
rows: What picture or sense does this make me see, hear or feel?
Why this word and not a plainer one?
What attitude does the speaker take?
What feeling is left with the reader?
How does the poem move from beginning to end?
Why this shape: stanzas, line length, rhyme or none?

teach.heading: Model: analysing a poem you have not seen
teach.note: I do. Read the short original poem aloud twice (it was written for this lesson, so it is not an exam poem): 'The bakery light comes on at four. Flour hangs in the air like slow snow. He lifts the trays with practised care, the heat a hand against his face. Outside, the city is still folded, its windows dark as closed books. He sets the loaves to cool, and waits for the first door to open.' Think aloud about the simile, the metaphor of the folded city and the ending. Stress: the effect on the reader is the engine of every sentence.

model.problem: How does the writer present the baker's working world in this original poem?
steps: Point: the writer presents the work as quiet, patient and hidden from others.
Evidence: the simile 'like slow snow' describes flour in the air.
Zoom: 'slow' suggests unhurried movement and 'snow' adds softness and stillness, so the bakery feels like its own calm world.
Link: this contrasts with the 'folded' city outside, where the windows are 'dark as closed books', so the baker seems the only person awake and giving.
model.answer: The writer presents the baker's work as quiet and patient. The simile 'like slow snow' describes the flour, and 'slow' suggests unhurried movement while 'snow' adds softness and stillness, so the bakery feels like a calm world of its own. This contrasts with the city outside, whose windows are 'dark as closed books', suggesting that everyone else is closed off and asleep while he quietly prepares food for them.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Pupils show answers on whiteboards. B is the target. A is feature-spotting, C is retelling, D drifts into context that this paper does not reward.

check.q: Which sentence shows AO2 at its best?
options: The poet uses a simile.
The simile 'like slow snow' makes the flour seem soft and still, so the bakery feels peaceful.
The baker gets up early and bakes bread.
Bakers in the past worked very hard for low pay.
check.why: Only B names a technique, quotes briefly and explains its effect. A names a technique with no effect, C retells the poem and D brings in outside context, which Section A does not reward.

teach.heading: Preparing: a modern poetry habit
teach.note: The specification says candidates should study a selection of modern poetry to prepare. Set up a routine: one new poem per week, three reads, three annotations, one sentence on effect. Suggest a mix of voices and cultures. Do not photocopy whole poems into notes for the exam: the poem will be printed on the paper. Remind pupils that tone and mood can be tracked with a simple word on the margin at each stanza.
bullets: One new modern poem a week
Read three times: gist, feeling, technique

practice: With a partner, find one lens from the focus list in the baker poem that we have not yet used (structure or form) and say what you notice.
Rewrite this weak sentence so it earns AO2: 'The poet uses a metaphor in line five.'
Decide whether this sentence is about AO2: 'The poem was probably written after the war.' Explain.
independent: Core: annotate the baker poem using at least four lenses, then write one PEE paragraph on the ending.
Extend: write a full opening paragraph that states an overview of the poem's tone and structure.
Stretch: explain how the poem's very short final line and the idea of waiting could be read in two different ways.
exit: State three facts about Section A.
Write one sentence about tone in the baker poem using a three-word quotation.
lessons.homework: Choose one modern poem from a poet you do not know. Read it three times and write four sentences on its imagery and tone. Do not copy any lines out in full.
lessons.send: SEND: give a lens card with sentence starters ('This makes the reader feel... because...'). EAL: pre-teach tone/mood vocabulary with images. Stretch: link form to meaning without being prompted.

lessons.unit: Unit 1B: Component 1 Section B: Anthology poetry (16 poems)
lessons.title: The anthology paper: 30 marks, AO2 and AO3 and how to know all 16 poems
lessons.bigQuestion: How do you get ready to compare two poems when you cannot choose them until you see the question?
objectives: State the format of Section B: one 30-mark question from two, comparing two anthology poems
Explain the 15 AO2 and 15 AO3 split and what each rewards
Group all 16 poems in the anthology by theme so any pair can be compared
successCriteria: All: name how many marks AO2 and AO3 carry in Section B
Most: group the 16 poems into at least four themes
Some: justify a comparison pair by naming a link of theme and a difference of method
lessons.crossCurricular: History and art: the anthology ranges from Shakespeare to modern poets
lessons.smsc: Social: hearing voices from different cultures and generations

keywords.def: a collection of poems by different writers; Part 3 of the Pearson anthology is the set text
analysis of language, form and structure
exploring links and connections between texts
showing how two poems are alike and different
an idea a poem explores
a point of view

starter: Bismillah. What does AO2 stand for in one phrase?
Name one poem from the anthology and its poet.
Give one way two poems can be linked.

teach.heading: What Section B asks
teach.note: Use the specification: Part 3 of the Pearson Edexcel International GCSE English Anthology; all 16 poems are studied; Component 1 is closed book but the anthology poems are provided in the exam. One 30-mark question, chosen from two, compares two anthology poems. Pupils do not need to memorise the poems word for word, but they must know them closely enough to find evidence fast. Tell the class to check the exact question wording against Pearson's specimen paper (verify).
bullets: Closed book; the poems are provided in the exam
One 30-mark question from a choice of two

teach.heading: 15 marks AO2, 15 marks AO3
teach.note: Draw the split on the board. AO2 is the analysis of language, form and structure and the effects. AO3 is exploring links and connections: themes, ideas, perspective, tone, structure. Equal marks means equal time: a paragraph on only one poem is lopsided. The trap: pupils write two separate essays glued together. Aim for integrated paragraphs with comparative connectives.

teach.heading: Mapping the 16 poems by theme
teach.note: Ask pupils to place each poem in at least one theme group before they look at the table. The groups are a revision aid, not the only way: many poems sit in several. Poems 1-8 are: If-, Prayer Before Birth, Blessing, Search For My Tongue, Half-past Two, Piano, Hide and Seek, Sonnet 116. Poems 9-16 are: La Belle Dame sans Merci, Poem at Thirty-Nine, War Photographer, The Tyger, My Last Duchess, Half-caste, Do not go gentle into that good night, Remember.

head: Theme
Poems that fit (not exhaustive)
rows: Half-past Two, Piano, Hide and Seek, Poem at Thirty-Nine
Search For My Tongue, Half-caste, Blessing
Sonnet 116, La Belle Dame sans Merci, Remember, Piano
My Last Duchess, The Tyger, War Photographer
Do not go gentle into that good night, Remember, Poem at Thirty-Nine
If-, Prayer Before Birth, Do not go gentle into that good night

teach.heading: Model: choosing a pair and a link
teach.note: I do. Choose Sonnet 116 and Remember as a pair about love and time. Say the link aloud, then one similarity of method (both are sonnets) and one difference (Shakespeare asserts permanent love; Rossetti imagines being forgotten). Show that a strong thesis sentence already contains AO2 and AO3.

model.problem: Plan a comparison of 'Sonnet 116' and 'Remember' on how poets present love and time.
steps: Link (AO3): both poems present love as something that has to face time and death.
Method (AO2): both are sonnets, so each uses a turn near the end to change the argument.
Difference (AO3): Shakespeare's speaker is certain that love cannot change; Rossetti's speaker accepts that the beloved may forget.
Judgement: one poem is a bold claim, the other a gentle permission.
model.answer: Both poets present love as tested by time, but they respond differently. Shakespeare's speaker confidently insists that love never alters, using a firm sonnet argument and a closing couplet to challenge any doubters. Rossetti's speaker, by contrast, speaks quietly and gives the beloved permission to forget, using the turn in the sonnet to move from a request to remember towards a kinder wish for happiness.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Pupils choose on whiteboards. C is the best AO3 sentence because it connects both poems.

check.q: Which sentence best earns AO3 marks?
options: 'War Photographer' is about a photographer.
'Piano' has three stanzas.
Both 'Piano' and 'Half-past Two' present childhood memory, but one is warm and the other uneasy.
'Hide and Seek' uses short lines.
check.why: C links two poems and compares tone. A and D describe one poem only; B states a feature without a link or an effect.

practice: Pick two poems from different theme groups. Find one surprising link between them.
Write a one-sentence thesis comparing two poems on the theme of identity.
Which of the 16 poems do you know least? Write one sentence about what it is about.
independent: Core: complete a grid of all 16 poems with theme, voice and form (one word each).
Extend: choose three pairs of poems and write a link sentence for each.
Stretch: argue why two poems from different groups make a better comparison than two from the same group.
exit: How many marks does AO3 carry in Section B?
Name two poems you could compare on childhood and give one link.
lessons.homework: Learn the titles and poets of all 16 poems and write one theme beside each from memory.
lessons.send: SEND: give a pre-filled blank grid with poem titles. EAL: provide a glossary of theme words. Stretch: compare a poem with another across three different themes.

lessons.title: If-: Kipling's advice, the conditional structure and the closing promise
lessons.bigQuestion: Is the advice in 'If-' wise, or is it an impossible standard?
objectives: Explain how Kipling uses a series of conditional clauses to build an argument
Analyse tone, voice and form in the poem
Connect the poem to its Edwardian context of stoicism
successCriteria: All: identify the repeated 'If' structure and say what it does
Most: explain the effect of the final line
Some: evaluate whether the voice is encouraging or demanding
lessons.crossCurricular: History: the British Empire and ideas of manliness; PSHE: resilience

keywords.def: a clause beginning with 'if' that sets up a possible situation
repetition of a word or phrase at the start of lines
calmly enduring hardship without complaint
speaking straight to the reader or listener
a statement that seems to contradict itself but reveals a truth
the pattern of rhyme at the ends of lines

starter: Bismillah. What does AO3 reward?
Define tone.
Name one poem from the anthology that gives advice or hope.

teach.heading: Who is speaking and to whom
teach.note: Kipling published the poem in 1910 and is said to have been inspired by Leander Starr Jameson (verify detail). The speaker is an older, wiser voice addressing a young listener, and the last line names 'my son', but pupils should see that the 'you' is also the reader. Ask: does the voice sound loving or commanding? Allow both readings. Note the poem is public domain so short quotation is fine.
bullets: Published 1910; written in the Edwardian period
Speaker is an older, authoritative voice
Direct address to 'you', and finally 'my son'

teach.heading: Form and structure
teach.note: The poem has four stanzas of eight lines each. Count them with the class. It has a regular rhyme pattern (ABABCDCD, check in class). Because the poem is one long sentence-like argument, with a series of 'If' clauses and one main clause held back until the end, tension builds. The payoff arrives in the final two lines: 'Yours is the Earth' and 'you'll be a Man, my son!'. Ask pupils why a regular rhyme scheme suits a poem about self-control.

timeline.label: Stanza 1
timeline.text: Keeping calm when others lose their heads and doubt you

timeline.label: Stanza 2
timeline.text: Dreams, thoughts and the way triumph and disaster are impostors

timeline.label: Stanza 3
timeline.text: Facing loss and starting again; will and endurance

timeline.label: Stanza 4
timeline.text: Dealing with crowds and kings; the reward in the last lines

teach.heading: Model: analysing the 'If' structure
teach.note: I do. Quote briefly: 'If you can keep your head'. Show how the conditional makes the reader think 'could I?' Link to tone: demanding yet hopeful. Point out paradoxes: treating 'Triumph and Disaster' the same.

model.problem: How does Kipling use structure to present the qualities of a good person in 'If-'?
steps: Point: he builds one long argument out of repeated conditions.
Evidence: the repeated 'If' at the start of many lines.
Zoom: the repetition (anaphora) piles up demands, so the reader feels how hard the ideal is, while the delayed main clause keeps the reader waiting for the reward.
Link: the final promise 'you'll be a Man, my son!' feels earned because the conditions have been long and hard.
model.answer: Kipling builds one long argument from repeated conditions. The repeated 'If' at the start of many lines piles up demands, so the reader feels how hard the ideal is, while the delay of the main clause keeps the reader waiting for the reward. The final promise that 'you'll be a Man, my son!' feels earned because the conditions have been so long and demanding.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Pupils respond on whiteboards. B is correct.

check.q: What is the main effect of repeating 'If'?
options: It shows the poet could not think of other words.
It builds a series of demands and keeps the reader waiting for the reward.
It makes the poem rhyme.
It shows the poet is angry.
check.why: B links the technique to its effect on the reader. A is unsupported, C confuses repetition with rhyme, D misreads the calm, measured tone.

teach.heading: Context and critical view
teach.note: The Edwardian ideal of a stoic, self-controlled man belongs to its time and to the idea of empire. A modern reader may notice the poem's gendered language ('Man', 'son') and ask whether the advice applies to everyone. Encourage an informed personal response (AO1-style engagement) but remember Section B is AO2 and AO3 only, so context supports links rather than being the focus. Compare with 'Prayer Before Birth' (voice and perspective) for AO3.
bullets: Keep the focus on method and effect

practice: Find two paradoxes or opposites in the poem and say what idea they support (no quotation longer than three words).
Why is the ending delayed until the last two lines?
Write a sentence comparing the voice in 'If-' with that of a poem you know.
independent: Core: write a PEE paragraph on the effect of repeated 'If' clauses.
Extend: analyse how the regular rhyme scheme links to the idea of self-control.
Stretch: write a comparison paragraph of 'If-' and 'Prayer Before Birth' focusing on voice and fear versus confidence.
exit: Name the structure Kipling uses at the start of many lines.
Is the tone of 'If-' encouraging, demanding or both? Support in one sentence.
lessons.homework: Write a four-line modern 'If' piece of advice for a Year 7, using at least two 'If' clauses and a final promise.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a stanza-by-stanza summary card. EAL: paraphrase the opening lines in simple English first. Stretch: evaluate the poem's gendered language and its impact on AO3 comparisons.

lessons.title: Sonnet 116: Shakespeare's definition of true love
lessons.bigQuestion: Can love really be unchanging, or is that a claim too good to be true?
objectives: Explain the argument of each quatrain and the couplet
Analyse metaphors of the star and the sea-mark and the personification of Time
Compare how the sonnet form shapes meaning
successCriteria: All: identify the sonnet's rhyme scheme and the final couplet
Most: explain two metaphors for love
Some: evaluate how the closing couplet works as a challenge
lessons.crossCurricular: History: Elizabethan love poetry; Maths: 14 lines, 3 quatrains and 1 couplet
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: steadfastness, commitment and faithfulness in marriage

keywords.def: a four-line group of lines
two rhyming lines, here closing the poem
giving human qualities to an idea or object
describing one thing as if it were another
a turn in argument or thought
a line of ten syllables in five stresses

starter: Bismillah. What is a metaphor?
How many lines does a Shakespearean sonnet have?
Define theme.

teach.heading: Form: the Shakespearean sonnet
teach.note: Show the structure: fourteen lines, three quatrains and a couplet, rhyming ABAB CDCD EFEF GG, in iambic pentameter. Quatrain 1 defines what love is not; quatrain 2 gives positive images; quatrain 3 brings in Time; the couplet stakes everything on the claim. Ask: what kind of poem is this, a love poem or an argument? Pupils may say both.
bullets: 14 lines: three quatrains and a couplet
Rhyme scheme ABAB CDCD EFEF GG
Iambic pentameter: ten syllables, five beats
Argument: definition, image, challenge to Time, claim

teach.heading: Image bank: the star and the sea-mark
teach.note: Brief quotations are permitted: Shakespeare is public domain. Love is 'an ever-fixed mark' that 'looks on tempests and is never shaken', and 'the star to every wandering bark'. Discuss: a sea-mark is a navigational landmark; a bark is a small ship. Love is the fixed point for the lost. Link to tone: confident, even defiant.

quote.text: It is the star to every wandering bark

teach.heading: Time and the sickle
teach.note: Time is personified as someone with a 'bending sickle', so love 'is not Time's fool'. Explain that 'compass' means range, so beauty falls within the sickle's reach but love does not. Ask pupils what the metaphor of a harvest suggests about time and death. Point to the shift in imagery from the sea to the field.
bullets: Time is personified as a reaper
Rosy lips and cheeks fall within its range
Love outlasts them: 'even to the edge of doom'

teach.heading: Model: analysing the couplet
teach.note: I do. The couplet 'If this be error and upon me proved, / I never writ, nor no man ever loved' stakes the poet's whole work on his claim. Show how the structure makes the speaker's confidence ring and how the double negative ('nor no man') emphasises certainty.

model.problem: How does Shakespeare present the permanence of love in the closing couplet?
steps: Point: he ends with a bold challenge that stakes everything on the claim.
Evidence: 'If this be error and upon me proved' sets up a condition; the second line says he 'never writ' and no man 'ever loved'.
Zoom: the couplet's rhyme gives a final, clinching sound, and the exaggerated claim that nobody has ever loved if he is wrong shows total confidence.
Link: the speaker's certainty seems almost defiant, as though he is arguing with an unseen doubter.
model.answer: Shakespeare ends with a bold challenge that stakes everything on his claim. The condition 'If this be error and upon me proved' sets up the possibility of being wrong, but the next line says that he 'never writ' and no man 'ever loved', an exaggerated claim that shows complete confidence. The rhyming couplet gives a final, clinching sound, so the speaker seems almost defiant, as though he is arguing with an unseen doubter.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Pupils answer on whiteboards. B is correct.

check.q: What is the best explanation of 'Love's not Time's fool'?
options: Love is stupid.
Love cannot be tricked or controlled by time.
Time is a fool.
Love is a joke.
check.why: B interprets the personification: love is not Time's puppet. A and D misread the idiom, C reverses the relationship.

practice: Which quatrain is mostly about what love is NOT, and which about what it IS?
Explain in your own words the image of the star and the ship.
Write a sentence comparing the confident tone here with the gentle tone of 'Remember'.
independent: Core: write a PEE paragraph on the star or sea-mark metaphor.
Extend: explain how Time is personified and why the imagery shifts to harvesting.
Stretch: argue whether the sonnet is a description of love or a defence of it.
exit: Name the rhyme scheme of the final couplet.
Write one sentence on what Time is compared to.
lessons.homework: Learn the four-part structure of the sonnet (definition, image, Time, couplet) and write one sentence for each part in your own words.
lessons.send: SEND: give a labelled sonnet diagram. EAL: give a glossary of 'bark', 'alter', 'impediment'. Stretch: compare the sonnet's use of Time with 'Do not go gentle into that good night'.

lessons.title: Remember: Rossetti's sonnet of farewell and the gift of forgetting
lessons.bigQuestion: Is it kinder to be remembered or to be forgotten?
objectives: Analyse the Petrarchan sonnet form and its turn
Explore tone and voice in a poem addressed to the person left behind
Compare Rossetti's approach to loss with another anthology poem
successCriteria: All: identify that the poem is a sonnet and where its turn occurs
Most: analyse the effect of repeated 'remember' and softening words
Some: compare Rossetti's treatment of loss with a poem such as 'Do not go gentle'
lessons.crossCurricular: History: Victorian poetry and its attitude to death; RE: remembrance in different faiths
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: mercy, acceptance and letting go

keywords.def: a sonnet with an octave (eight lines) and a sestet (six lines)
the first eight lines
the last six lines
the turn in argument
using a word more than once for effect
a poem of mourning

starter: Bismillah. Define the term 'volta'.
What is the difference between Shakespearean and Petrarchan sonnets?
Name one poem in the anthology that deals with death.

teach.heading: The situation
teach.note: Rossetti wrote the poem in 1849 and published it in 1862 (verify dates in a reliable source). The speaker is dying or going away and speaks directly to someone she loves. She asks to be remembered, but later changes her request. Ask: whose feelings does the poem prioritise? Note that Rossetti is public domain, so short quotations are fine.
bullets: She is facing death or separation
Tone moves from request to reassurance

teach.heading: Form: octave and sestet
teach.note: The poem is a Petrarchan sonnet: an octave rhyming ABBA ABBA, and a sestet with a different pattern (check the rhyme scheme in class). The octave asks the beloved to remember, while the sestet begins with 'Yet if you should forget me for a while' (the volta) and ends with a generous reversal. Link the form to meaning: the turn mirrors the speaker's change of heart.

left.title: Octave (lines 1-8)
points: Memories of shared life and plans

right.title: Sestet (lines 9-14)
points: Ending: better to forget and smile

teach.heading: Language: repetition and softening
teach.note: Pupils highlight the repeated 'remember' in the opening and the final lines' pairing of 'forget and smile' with 'remember and be sad'. Discuss how the balance of the last two lines (a parallel structure) makes the speaker's wish feel measured and kind. 'Silent land' is a euphemism for death.
bullets: Parallel final lines: smile versus sad

teach.heading: Model: analysing the volta
teach.note: I do. Use the sestet's opening: 'Yet if you should forget me for a while'. Show how 'Yet' pivots the poem and 'for a while' makes forgetting temporary and forgivable.

model.problem: How does Rossetti present the speaker's changing attitude towards being remembered?
steps: Point: she moves from asking to be remembered to freeing the beloved from grief.
Evidence: the octave opens with 'Remember me' while the sestet begins 'Yet if you should forget me for a while'.
Zoom: 'Yet' marks the turn, and 'for a while' treats forgetting as understandable and temporary, so the tone becomes tender and unselfish.
Link: the final lines, 'forget and smile' set against 'remember and be sad', make her prefer the beloved's happiness to her own memory.
model.answer: Rossetti presents a speaker who moves from asking to be remembered to freeing her beloved from grief. The octave opens with 'Remember me', but the sestet begins 'Yet if you should forget me for a while'. 'Yet' marks the turn, and 'for a while' treats forgetting as understandable and temporary, so the tone becomes tender and unselfish. The final lines set 'forget and smile' against 'remember and be sad', showing that she prefers her beloved's happiness to her own memory.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Pupils respond with whiteboards. C is the best.

check.q: Where is the volta in 'Remember' and what does it do?
options: Line 1: it introduces the speaker.
Line 8: it ends the poem.
Line 9: it turns from a request to be remembered to a wish for the beloved's happiness.
Line 14: it repeats the first line.
check.why: The sestet begins with 'Yet', turning the poem. A and B misplace the turn; D confuses the ending with the structure.

practice: Say what 'silent land' means and why a poet might choose it.
Find one word in the octave that sounds like a command or request.
Compare the tone at the start and at the end in one sentence each.
independent: Core: write a PEE paragraph on the volta.
Extend: analyse the parallel structure of the last two lines.
Stretch: write a comparison paragraph with 'Do not go gentle into that good night', contrasting acceptance with resistance.
exit: Where does the sonnet turn?
Write one sentence about the final line's tone.
lessons.homework: Write a 10-minute comparison plan for 'Remember' and 'Do not go gentle into that good night': one link, two differences, one quotation each (max 3 words).
lessons.send: SEND: give a labelled sonnet frame. EAL: glossary of 'counsel', 'vestige', 'grieve' (check the actual words in the printed poem). Stretch: evaluate how the poem could be read as a faith-informed acceptance.

lessons.unit: Unit 1C: Component 1 Section C: Modern prose (choose one text)
lessons.title: Closed-book prose: preparing to write about a novel without the text
lessons.bigQuestion: How can you write precisely about a novel when the book is not on your desk?
objectives: State the Section C rules: closed book, 40 marks, 20 AO1 and 20 AO4
Build a compact bank of references to key moments rather than long quotations
Plan an answer from memory in five minutes
successCriteria: All: say that Section C is closed book and no text is allowed
Most: create a bank of five key moments with short references
Some: plan a full essay from memory using chapter or event references
lessons.crossCurricular: Memory techniques and study skills; PSHE: revision habits
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: trust (tawakkul) combined with effort in preparation

keywords.def: an exam where you may not bring the text
a short list of brief, useful quotations
a pointer to a moment or detail in the text without quoting it in full
expressing an idea in your own words
close knowledge, critical style and informed personal engagement
understanding links between the text and its contexts

starter: Bismillah. What does AO4 assess?
Name two things a topic sentence should do.
List the 7 Pearson prose options as far as you can.

teach.heading: The rules of Section C
teach.note: State the specification facts: one 40-mark question from a choice of two for each text; marks split 20 for AO1 and 20 for AO4; closed book, so texts are not allowed. Pearson prescribes no edition for the closed-book prose because pupils will not have the text in the exam, though recommended editions appear in Appendix 3 (verify before buying copies). Tell pupils: you do not need to quote at length, you need to know the book.
bullets: Closed book: no texts in the exam

teach.heading: What 'knowledge' means without the book
teach.note: Teach the hierarchy of evidence: best is a precise short quotation of three to six words; next is a close reference to an event, character action or structural moment; weakest is a vague summary. Pupils should be able to cite scene, chapter or section accurately. Accuracy of detail matters more than length. Never invent a quotation: a precise paraphrase scores better than a wrong quotation.

head: Level of evidence
Example (for a generic novel)
Quality
rows: 'at the end of chapter 6, he returns to the river'

teach.heading: Building a memory bank
teach.note: Use the 'five moments' method: opening, a turning point, a moment of conflict, the climax and the ending. For each, record the character, the event, one theme, one writer's method and one context link. Add three exact short quotations per text. Test by retrieval, not re-reading. Ask pupils to say each moment aloud without notes.

teach.heading: Model: planning an answer from memory
teach.note: I do. Use a generic text, or your class text. Show how a plan in a few lines can include a thesis, three moments with a method each, one context point each and a conclusion. Say it aloud in two minutes.

model.problem: Plan a response to: 'How does the writer present the importance of friendship?' (for any set text).
steps: Thesis: friendship is shown as the main source of hope and also a source of risk.
Moment 1 (opening): shows the bond; method: dialogue or setting; context: a world where friendship is rare.
Moment 2 (turning point): the friendship is tested; method: structure or tension; context: a social pressure.
Moment 3 (ending): outcome and message; method: symbolism or tone; context: writer's purpose.
Conclusion: the writer's view of friendship across the whole text.
model.answer: A plan lists a thesis, three moments each with a method and a context point, and a conclusion: it should fit on five lines and take five minutes. Writing this plan before the first paragraph keeps an unaided essay focused on the question and secures both AO1 and AO4.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Pupils answer on whiteboards. B is correct.

check.q: In a closed-book Section C answer, which is best?
options: A long quotation copied from memory with a few errors.
An accurate short quotation plus a precise reference to where it happens.
A vague summary of the plot.
A context fact with no link to the text.
check.why: B is accurate and linked. A risks errors and wastes time, C lacks specificity and D is a bolt-on that cannot earn AO4 without a link to the text.

practice: Write the five moments for the text you are studying, one line each.
Turn a long quotation you know into a three-word exact quotation.
Give one reason why a wrong quotation is worse than a paraphrase.
independent: Core: complete a five-moment bank for your text, with one theme and method for each moment.
Extend: add three exact quotations of up to six words each, with chapter references.
Stretch: write a two-minute spoken plan for a question about family or power, then check it with a partner.
exit: What are the marks for AO1 and AO4 in Section C?
State one way to show knowledge without quoting at length.
lessons.homework: Complete your five-moment bank and learn the references; bring the plan to the next lesson for a quick-fire test.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a ready-made five-moment template. EAL: allow spoken plans first. Stretch: link each moment to a different AO4 context type.

lessons.unit: Unit 1C: Component 1 Section C: Modern prose (choose one text)
lessons.title: AO4 in prose: the kinds of context and how readers receive a text over time
lessons.bigQuestion: Does a novel mean the same thing to every generation of readers?
objectives: Identify the kinds of context named in the specification: writer's life, historical setting, social and cultural attitudes
Explain literary context and reception over time
Choose a context type that suits the question
successCriteria: All: name three kinds of context for a novel
Most: link a context fact to a writer's choice
Some: explain how readers' responses to a text have changed over time
lessons.crossCurricular: History and sociology: how attitudes change; RE: reading texts in historical context
lessons.smsc: Social and cultural: understanding that people hold different values at different times

keywords.def: the circumstances in which a text was written, set or received
the genres and writing traditions a text belongs to
how different audiences respond to a text over time
the beliefs of a society about people and behaviour
the time and place in which a story happens
the writer's reason for writing

starter: Bismillah. Define context in your own words.
What does a bolt-on context fact look like?
Name the setting (time and place) of the prose text you are studying.

teach.heading: The five kinds of AO4 context
teach.note: Teach from the specification: AO4 context includes the writer's life, historical setting, and social and cultural attitudes; it also includes literary context and how different audiences receive the text over time. Make clear that it is not five boxes to fill: choose the one or two that illuminate the question. Pupils must link them to the writer's choices.

head: Type
Ask yourself
Example (brief)
rows: What in the author's experience shaped this?
Steinbeck worked on California ranches as a young man
What was happening in the time and place?
What did people believe about race, class, gender, tradition?
Colonial attitudes in Things Fall Apart
What genre or tradition is this part of?
A coming-of-age story; a response to earlier colonial fiction
How have readers reacted over time?
Some texts have been praised, challenged or reread differently

teach.heading: Literary context and reception
teach.note: Literary context means the writing traditions around a text: for example, Things Fall Apart is often read as a response to earlier European stories about Africa (Achebe criticised Conrad in a 1975 lecture; verify detail), while Klara and the Sun belongs with near-future science fiction. Reception: some texts have been challenged or removed from schools in different periods and places, and readers today may see race, gender or class differently. Tell pupils to use reception sparingly and carefully, with accurate facts only.
bullets: Always link back to the text

teach.heading: Model: linking historical setting to a method
teach.note: I do. Use Of Mice and Men: the Great Depression made migrant workers precarious. The recurring dream of owning land in the novella is a response to this insecurity, so the dream feels both precious and fragile.

model.problem: How is the idea of the American Dream presented in Of Mice and Men (use context)?
steps: Point: Steinbeck presents the dream of owning land as a fragile hope.
Evidence: George and Lennie repeatedly talk about their own place and 'the rabbits'.
Zoom: set in the Great Depression, when migrant workers had little security, this dream seems both desperate and touching; the repeated talk shows how much they need it.
Link: the ending, where the dream cannot survive, suggests that Steinbeck criticises a society that offers few chances.
model.answer: Steinbeck presents the dream of owning land as a fragile hope. George and Lennie repeatedly talk about their own place and the rabbits, and because the novella is set in the Great Depression, when migrant workers had little security, this dream seems both desperate and touching. The ending, where the dream cannot survive, suggests that Steinbeck is criticising a society that offers working men few chances.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Pupils answer on whiteboards. C is correct.

options: The writer was born in 1926.
The story is set in a small town.
Later readers have reread the novel in the light of new debates about race and justice.
The novel has three parts.
check.why: Only C describes how audiences respond over time. A is writer's life, B is setting and D is structure.

practice: Match each context type to one fact for your set text.
Write one sentence linking a historical fact to a writer's choice.
Explain how a modern reader's view of your text might differ from the first readers.
independent: Core: write context notes (one line each) for the writer, historical setting and social attitudes of your text.
Extend: add a literary context point and a reception point.
Stretch: write a paragraph that weaves two kinds of context into an analysis of one moment.
exit: Name two AO4 context types.
Give one way reception could change how we read a novel.
lessons.homework: Write one 100-word paragraph on your set text weaving in one kind of context and one short quotation.
lessons.send: SEND: use a colour-coded context table. EAL: pre-teach 'reception' with examples. Stretch: write a paragraph that argues context is more or less important to your text.

lessons.unit: Unit 1C-OPT: Modern prose options listed by Pearson Edexcel
lessons.title: Set texts: To Kill a Mockingbird and Of Mice and Men
lessons.bigQuestion: How do two American novels show injustice and the cost of being different?
objectives: Summarise the plot, setting and narrative method of each text
Explain two key themes in each text
Link each text to context without long quotation
successCriteria: All: summarise plot and setting of each text
Most: explain a theme in each text with a reference
Some: compare how each text presents prejudice and loneliness
lessons.crossCurricular: History: segregation and the Great Depression; Citizenship: justice and rights
lessons.smsc: Moral: justice, compassion and standing up for the vulnerable

keywords.def: the voice telling the story
forced separation of people by race
a worker who moves from place to place for work
an object or idea that stands for something bigger
a short novel
an unfair opinion formed without good reason

starter: Bismillah. What does AO4 assess?
What is a symbol?
Give one reason why a writer sets a story in the past.

teach.heading: To Kill a Mockingbird: the basics
teach.note: Harper Lee, published 1960. Set in Maycomb, a small Alabama town, in the 1930s. Narrated by Scout Finch looking back on childhood, so the voice combines a child's innocence with adult hindsight. Atticus Finch, a lawyer, defends Tom Robinson, a Black man accused of a crime against a white woman. Boo Radley is the neighbour the children fear and later understand. The novel has two parts, 31 chapters. Atticus's empathy advice is in chapter 3; the 'sin to kill a mockingbird' idea comes in chapter 10; the trial is in chapters 17-21 (verify chapter numbers in class edition). Quote only short phrases.
bullets: Themes: prejudice, justice, empathy, growing up

teach.heading: Of Mice and Men: the basics
teach.note: John Steinbeck, 1937. A short novella of six chapters, set in California's Salinas Valley during the Great Depression. George and Lennie, two migrant workers, share a dream of owning a small farm. Characters include Candy, Crooks, Curley and Curley's wife, and Slim. The story is told by a third-person narrator who stays outside the characters' minds. The first and last chapters take place by the river, giving a circular structure. The title comes from a poem by Robert Burns about plans that go wrong.
bullets: Circular structure: river at start and end

teach.heading: Compare the two texts
teach.note: Use the table to prepare for a question on social injustice. Ask: who has no power in each community? Pupils should be able to cite one event for each point. Avoid long quotation; refer to scenes.

head: Aspect
To Kill a Mockingbird
Of Mice and Men
rows: The farm dream and the rabbits

teach.heading: Model: a paragraph without long quotation
teach.note: I do. Use scenes and a short phrase. Show that a reference to the trial and a three-word quotation can earn full AO1 credit.

model.problem: How does Harper Lee present prejudice in To Kill a Mockingbird?
steps: Point: Lee presents prejudice as built into the justice system of Maycomb.
Evidence: in the trial (chapters 17-21 in many editions), Tom Robinson is convicted despite Atticus showing the evidence is weak.
Zoom: Scout's child's view makes the injustice feel plain and shocking, while the jury's verdict shows the strength of racial attitudes.
Link: Lee's 1960 readers faced the civil rights movement, so the trial challenges them to examine their own attitudes.
model.answer: Lee presents prejudice as built into the justice system of Maycomb. In the trial, Tom Robinson is convicted even though Atticus shows that the evidence is weak. Scout's child's-eye view makes the injustice feel plain and shocking, while the jury's verdict shows how strong racial attitudes are. Because the novel was published in 1960, in the era of the civil rights movement, Lee seems to challenge her readers to examine their own attitudes.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Pupils answer on whiteboards. A is correct.

check.q: What is the best description of the narration of Of Mice and Men?
options: Third person, observing events from outside characters' minds.
First person narrated by George.
Letters between the characters.
First person narrated by Lennie.
check.why: The novella uses a third-person, camera-like narrator. B and D wrongly assume a character narrator and C invents a form.

practice: Write a two-sentence summary of each text without using a name.
Name one symbol in each text and what it stands for.
Which text would you prefer to write about and why?
independent: Core: complete the comparison table with one scene reference per box.
Extend: write a paragraph on loneliness in Of Mice and Men using a reference and a three-word quotation.
Stretch: compare how the two writers use setting to show who has power.
exit: Name the setting and narrator of each text.
State one context point for each text.
lessons.homework: Write a 120-word response to 'How does the writer present outsiders?' for your text, using one scene and one short quotation.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a character relationship map. EAL: read key chapter summaries with glossaries. Stretch: evaluate whether a child narrator or a third-person narrator is more effective for showing injustice.

lessons.unit: Unit 1C-OPT: Modern prose options listed by Pearson Edexcel
lessons.title: Set texts: Things Fall Apart and The Whale Rider
lessons.bigQuestion: What happens to a community when old traditions meet new pressures?
objectives: Summarise plot, setting and narrative method of each text
Explain how each text presents tradition, change and leadership
Link each text to its cultural context without long quotation
successCriteria: All: describe the setting and main characters of each text
Most: explain how each presents tradition and change
Some: compare how the two novels treat the idea of who may lead
lessons.crossCurricular: History: colonialism in Nigeria; Māori culture and the Treaty of Waitangi; RE: tradition and faith
lessons.smsc: Social and cultural: respecting other cultures and their stories

keywords.def: customs passed down through generations
one country taking control of another
a group of related families
stories and wisdom passed on by speaking
a society led by men
a traditional story about ancestors or gods

starter: Bismillah. Define colonialism.
What does 'oral tradition' mean?
Why might a writer use words from another language?

teach.heading: Things Fall Apart: the basics
teach.note: Chinua Achebe, 1958. Set in Umuofia, an Igbo village community in what is now Nigeria, in the late 19th century as British missionaries and administrators arrive. Okonkwo, a proud and fearful warrior, tries to avoid his father's reputation for weakness. The novel has three parts: traditional life; Okonkwo's exile; the arrival of colonial power and his tragic end. The title comes from a poem by W B Yeats. Achebe uses proverbs and Igbo words to give the voice of the community. (Verify chapter numbers in class edition.) Achebe, born 1930, was himself Igbo and lived through the end of British rule in Nigeria, which became independent in 1960.

teach.heading: The Whale Rider: the basics
teach.note: Witi Ihimaera, 1987. Set in Whangara, on the east coast of New Zealand's North Island, among Māori communities. Kahu, a young girl, is the descendant of Paikea, the legendary ancestor who rode a whale to shore. Her grandfather Koro Apirana believes leadership must pass to a boy, rejecting Kahu, while her grandmother Nanny Flowers stands by her. The narration mixes Rawiri's first-person voice with the passages in the voice of the whales. The climax involves a stranded pod of whales and Kahu's bond with them. Ihimaera is Māori.
bullets: Māori traditions and legend of Paikea
Kahu versus Koro's view of leadership
Two voices: Rawiri and the whales

teach.heading: Compare: tradition and change
teach.note: Pupils need a clear view of how each novel treats tradition: Achebe shows its richness and its rigidity before colonial change; Ihimaera shows a tradition under pressure from inside, as a girl proves herself a leader. Prompt a discussion about whether tradition can adapt.

left.title: Things Fall Apart
points: Change comes from outside: missionaries, courts

right.title: The Whale Rider
points: Pressure comes from within the family
Kahu proves leadership in new form

teach.heading: Model: a paragraph linking structure and context
teach.note: I do. Show how the three-part structure of Things Fall Apart reinforces the theme of change. Mention a reference rather than quoting.

model.problem: How does Achebe present the effects of colonial change in Things Fall Apart?
steps: Point: Achebe shows colonial change splitting a close community.
Evidence: in part three, missionaries win converts, including Okonkwo's son Nwoye, and the court of the colonial administration replaces clan justice.
Zoom: the three-part structure moves from a confident society to loss, so readers see what is lost before it is changed.

Link: Achebe wrote after independence movements grew and wanted to present Igbo society from the inside; the ending, in which the District Commissioner reduces Okonkwo to a few paragraphs in a book, criticises colonial attitudes.
model.answer: Achebe shows colonial change splitting a close community. In part three, missionaries win converts, including Okonkwo's son Nwoye, and a colonial court replaces clan justice. The three-part structure moves from a confident society to loss, so readers understand what is being lost. Achebe wrote on the eve of independence and wanted to present Igbo society from the inside; the ending, in which the District Commissioner reduces Okonkwo to a few paragraphs in a book, criticises colonial attitudes.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Pupils answer on whiteboards. C is correct.

check.q: In The Whale Rider, which conflict is central?
options: Two rival families fight over land.
A whaling company wants to hunt whales.
Koro Apirana's view of leadership clashes with Kahu's place as the heir in spirit.
A school wants to ban Māori language.
check.why: The central tension is between Koro's expectation of a male leader and Kahu's calling. A, B and D are not the core conflict.

practice: Write one sentence on how the setting shapes each novel.
Name one example of tradition in each text.
Explain why the District Commissioner's final thoughts matter (reference only).
independent: Core: complete a table of themes with one scene reference per text.
Extend: write a paragraph on leadership in The Whale Rider using reference and a three-word quote.
Stretch: compare how Achebe and Ihimaera use community voice to present change.
exit: Name the setting of each novel.
State one context point about each.
lessons.homework: Write 120 words on the question 'How does the writer present tradition?' for your text, using one reference and one context point.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a glossary of Igbo and Māori terms used in class (check in the edition). EAL: allow glossary in home language. Stretch: evaluate whether Achebe or Ihimaera is more optimistic about the future.

lessons.unit: Unit 1C-OPT: Modern prose options listed by Pearson Edexcel
lessons.title: Set texts: The Joy Luck Club and Western Lane (family, culture and grief)
lessons.bigQuestion: How do families carry stories, silence and loss between generations?
objectives: Summarise the structure and narrative method of each text
Explain how each text presents family, culture and grief
Link each text to cultural context using references, not long quotations
successCriteria: All: describe the narrators and family set-up in each text
Most: explain how each writer presents family tension
Some: compare how structure and narration shape the reader's response
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography/history: migration and diaspora; PSHE: bereavement and family
lessons.smsc: Social and cultural: understanding immigrant families and loss; Spiritual: patience (sabr) in grief

keywords.def: people who live away from their homeland
differences between older and younger family members
a short, descriptive scene or story
narration using 'I'
deep sorrow, especially after a death
using few words and simple style

starter: Bismillah. What does first-person narration do?
Define diaspora.
Give one way a short story can be connected to others in a novel.

teach.heading: The Joy Luck Club: the basics
teach.note: Amy Tan, 1989. The novel is made of sixteen linked stories in four sections, told by four Chinese immigrant mothers (Suyuan, An-mei, Lindo, Ying-ying) and their American-born daughters (Jing-mei, Rose, Waverly, Lena). The mothers meet to play mah-jong in San Francisco. Jing-mei takes her late mother Suyuan's place and journeys to China to meet her half-sisters. Tan was born in California to Chinese immigrant parents. The structure gives each voice equal weight; themes include culture clash, communication and identity. Quote only short phrases.

teach.heading: Western Lane: the basics
teach.note: Chetna Maroo, debut novel 2023 (shortlisted for the Booker Prize that year; verify). A new Pearson set text, first taught 2024 and assessed from May 2026. Narrated in first person by Gopi, a young girl from a British Gujarati family who has lost her mother. She and her sisters train in squash with their father, and the game becomes a way of coping with silence and grief. The style is spare and quiet. Context: British Gujarati family life, sport, bereavement (verify details in the class edition).

teach.heading: Compare: how each writer shapes our response
teach.note: Ask pupils to compare structure. Tan uses many voices in linked stories, so understanding builds by comparison. Maroo uses a single young voice with limited understanding, so the reader fills gaps. Both show what is unsaid within families.

teach.heading: Model: structure and meaning
teach.note: I do. Use Joy Luck Club structure; show how linked stories reveal parallel mother-daughter misunderstandings.

model.problem: How does Tan use structure to present mother-daughter relationships?
steps: Point: Tan uses linked stories to show that every pair misunderstands each other in a similar way.
Evidence: each section gives voices to mothers and daughters, such as Jing-mei's final journey to China.
Zoom: the many narrators let the reader see both sides, so the reader understands more than any single character.
Link: this reflects the immigrant experience of divided cultures, and Jing-mei's journey completes the circle by giving her mother's story an ending.
model.answer: Tan uses linked stories to show that each mother-daughter pair misunderstands the other in a similar way. Each section gives voices to both mothers and daughters, so the reader understands more than any single character. This reflects the immigrant experience of divided cultures, and Jing-mei's final journey to China completes the circle by giving her mother's story an ending.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Pupils answer on whiteboards. B is correct.

check.q: What is the effect of Gopi's young first-person narration in Western Lane?
options: It gives an adult's complete explanation.
It lets the reader notice what Gopi does not fully understand or say.
It makes the story funny.
It removes all emotion.
check.why: B explains the effect of a limited narrator. A reverses the effect, C and D misdescribe the tone.

practice: Write one sentence on how each family is affected by loss.
Say how the structure of each text is different.
Name one cultural detail from each text.
independent: Core: complete the comparison table with a reference from each text.
Extend: write a paragraph on silence in Western Lane using one reference and a short phrase.
Stretch: compare how the two novels present the idea that cultures are carried through family stories.
exit: How many narrators does each text have (approximately)?
State one theme common to both texts.

lessons.send: SEND: provide a character map. EAL: use bilingual summaries (verify details). Stretch: evaluate whether a single narrator or multiple narrators gives a fuller picture of a family.

Explain how Ishiguro presents love, loyalty and what makes us human
Link the text to science-fiction context and to Ishiguro's life
successCriteria: All: describe Klara's role and narrative viewpoint
Most: explain how limited perception shapes the reader's response
Some: evaluate Ishiguro's presentation of hope in a world of technology
lessons.crossCurricular: Science and computing: artificial intelligence and gene editing; RE: faith and what makes a human
lessons.smsc: Moral: love, loyalty, responsibility and the limits of technology

the story is told by Klara as 'I'
the narrator sees only part of the world
describing an imagined society where things have gone wrong
strong belief or trust

Give one example of unreliable or limited narration.
Why might a writer choose a robot as narrator?

teach.heading: The basics
teach.note: Kazuo Ishiguro, published 2021 (he won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2017). Klara is an Artificial Friend, bought to keep company with Josie, a teenager who is ill. Klara narrates in the first person and observes the world with simple, careful attention. The Sun is a source of nourishing energy for Klara and becomes a kind of god-like figure to her. Rick is Josie's friend; Josie's Mother makes a difficult plan. Pearson lists it as a new set text, first taught 2024 and first assessed in May 2026. Keep to short phrases when quoting.
bullets: Josie is ill; the Mother makes a plan

teach.heading: Narration and structure
teach.note: Klara sees the world in boxes at times, as if her vision is divided into panels, a method that shows her different way of seeing (verify exact detail in class edition). Her narration is polite and curious but limited, so readers notice what she does not fully understand about adult motives. The novel is told in parts: Klara in the shop, in Josie's home, and later in a quiet ending in the Yard. Ask: what do we know that Klara does not?

teach.heading: Themes and context
teach.note: Key themes: love and loyalty, faith in something greater, loneliness, and what makes humans unique. Context: ongoing debates about artificial intelligence and gene editing in the 2020s; Ishiguro was born in Nagasaki in 1954 and has lived in Britain since 1960, which may inform his interest in memory and displacement (verify). Literary context: science fiction and the 'Frankenstein' tradition of created beings. Reception: discussed widely as a novel about technology and tenderness.

teach.heading: Model: AO1 and AO4 together
teach.note: I do. Use reference only. Show a point about Klara's faith in the Sun and link to context.

model.problem: How does Ishiguro present faith in Klara and the Sun?
steps: Point: he presents Klara's faith as sincere and childlike, which makes it moving.
Evidence: Klara believes that the Sun can heal Josie, and she makes a promise to it.
Zoom: because Klara has a limited view of the world, her faith seems both pure and uncertain; the reader knows that the Sun's power is not proven.
Link: in an age of technology and artificial intelligence, Ishiguro asks whether faith and love can exist in a machine and what that says about humans.
model.answer: Ishiguro presents Klara's faith as sincere and childlike, which makes it moving. Klara believes that the Sun can heal Josie and makes a promise to it. Because Klara's view of the world is limited, her faith seems both pure and uncertain, since the reader knows the Sun's power is not proven. In an age of technology and artificial intelligence, Ishiguro asks whether faith and love can exist in a machine and what that says about humans.

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Pupils answer on whiteboards. B is correct.

check.q: Why does Ishiguro use Klara as a first-person narrator?
options: So the story can be a technical manual.
To show human life through a loyal, limited outsider.
So there is no emotion in the novel.
To avoid describing the setting.
check.why: B explains the effect: Klara sees people with fresh eyes. A, C and D contradict the text.

practice: Write two sentences summarising the plot of Klara and the Sun.
Name two things Klara notices that humans ignore (reference only).
Explain why the title includes 'the Sun'.
independent: Core: write a paragraph on Klara's loyalty using a reference and a three-word phrase.
Extend: add one context link to artificial intelligence or gene editing.
Stretch: evaluate whether the ending is hopeful or sad.
exit: Name Klara's role and her narrator position.
Give one context point for the novel.
lessons.homework: Write 120 words on 'How does Ishiguro present love?' with a reference and one context point.
lessons.send: SEND: provide a chapter summary map. EAL: glossary of 'Artificial Friend', 'lifting'. Stretch: compare Klara with another artificial being in literature.

teach.note: The specification's literary heritage list does not include A Christmas Carol, so the existing school lessons on it are written to AQA 8702 and cannot be assessed here. This does not make the text pointless: it is a short, clear Dickens text useful as wider reading. Explain the board change plainly so pupils see no waste: the skills transfer. Tell pupils that the closest Pearson option for Dickens is Great Expectations.

AQA 8702 material cannot be assessed here
It can stay as wider reading
Great Expectations is the Dickens option

teach.heading: Two Dickens texts side by side
teach.note: Use the table to show what carries across. A Christmas Carol is a novella (1843) of five staves with a third-person narrator. Great Expectations was serialised in 1860-61 and is a first-person retrospective novel following Pip from orphan boy to gentleman and a wiser adult. Dickens revised the ending after advice from a friend (verify detail). Pupils will see transferable skills.

head: Feature
A Christmas Carol
Great Expectations
rows: Pip learns from pride and snobbery
Pip, Estella, Miss Havisham, Magwitch, Joe

teach.note: Show how knowing A Christmas Carol helps with Great Expectations: Victorian poverty, social class, the effect of money on character and the moral journey. model.problem: How does a setting reflect a character in a Dickens text?
steps: Point: Dickens uses settings to mirror characters' states of mind.
Evidence: in A Christmas Carol, Scrooge's cold, dark rooms; in Great Expectations, Miss Havisham's decaying Satis House with its stopped clocks.
Zoom: both settings show a character stuck in the past or shut off from others, so the setting becomes a symbol of their inner life.
Link: the reader is invited to see that wealth does not guarantee happiness.
model.answer: Dickens uses settings to mirror characters' states of mind. Scrooge's cold, dark rooms show a man shut off from others, while Miss Havisham's decaying Satis House, with its stopped clocks, shows a woman stuck in the past. In both texts the setting becomes a symbol of inner life, inviting readers to see that wealth does not guarantee happiness.
